a OurBigBook.com
At a differentiable interior stationary point, all first-order changes of the scalar field vanish. In particular, the directional derivative along each coordinate axis vanishes, so fx​=fy​=0 and hence ∇f=0. Equivalently, the first-order differential df=∇f⋅dr vanishes for every displacement. A differentiable interior maximum or minimum must satisfy this condition; a stationary point need not be an extremum.
The standard nondegenerate local contour plot models are −x2−y2 for a maximum, x2+y2 for a minimum, and x2−y2 for a saddle point of a scalar function. Near a maximum, nested contours have lower values farther from the centre; near a minimum they have higher values. Near a saddle, hyperbolas occur on opposite sides of the critical level, whose contour has two intersecting tangent directions. More general nondegenerate quadratic forms deform these circles into ellipses; degenerate stationary points can have more complicated contours.

For 0<c<1, the contours are ellipses centred at (0,1/c), shrinking to the maximum as c↑1. The zero contour is the parabola from part (c). For −1<c<0, the contours are vertical-opening hyperbolas. For the heat equation Θt​=κΘxx​, separation of variables with homogeneous Neumann boundary condition at both ends gives spatial modes cos(nπx/L) and decay factors e−κ(nπ/L)2t. The n=0 mode is constant and does not decay.
The initial profile already contains only two such modes:
T0​sin2Lπx​=2T0​​−2T0​​cosL2πx​.
(111)
Evolving each mode therefore yields
Θ(x,t)=2T0​​[1−e−4κπ2t/L2cosL2πx​].​
(112)
The endpoint derivatives vanish, and substitution checks both the equation and the initial profile. The spatial integral remains LT0​/2: no heat escapes through insulated ends, so the limiting uniform temperature is T0​/2.

With homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition, the eigenfunctions are sin(nπx/L) and all modes decay. Write
Θ(x,t)=∑n=1∞​bn​sinLnπx​e−κ(nπ/L)2t,bn​=L2T0​​∫0L​sin2Lπx​sinLnπx​dx.
(113)
Reflection about the midpoint makes every even-n coefficient zero. For odd n, putting u=πx/L and using the product-to-sum identity gives
bn​​=π2T0​​∫0π​sin2usin(nu)du=π2T0​​[n1​−21​(n+21​+n−21​)]=πn(4−n2)8T0​​.​
(114)
In particular b1​=8T0​/(3π) and b3​=−8T0​/(15π). Thus
Θ(x,t)=π8T0​​m=0∑∞​(2m+1)[4−(2m+1)2]sin((2m+1)πx/L)​e−κ(2m+1)2π2t/L2.​
(115)
This uses the Fourier sine series of a squared sine. The coefficients are O(n−3), so the initial series converges uniformly; for t>0 the exponential factors also justify termwise differentiation to check the heat equation. Every mode vanishes at both endpoints, and the initial series gives the specified profile. Unlike part (a), there is no constant mode: the temperature tends to zero, with leading long-time term
Θ(x,t)∼3π8T0​​sinLπx​e−κπ2t/L2.
